claims.text: Adding 10–15 wt% tungsten or molybdenum to a nickel-based superalloy will stabilize its high-temperature microstructure.
The refractory-element addition will produce a predictable reduction in yield stress at high temperature.
The refractory-element addition will produce controlled creep behavior at high temperature.
The initial nickel-based superalloy has a polycrystalline, stabilized microstructure.
Near the alloy's homologous temperature, thermally activated dislocation climb and creep are active.
Tungsten or molybdenum alloying refines or stabilizes the precipitate distribution.
Tungsten or molybdenum alloying inhibits dislocation motion.
High-melting refractory elements impede thermally activated dislocation climb and creep by stabilizing the microstructure.
Microstructural stabilization ensures that yield stress decreases predictably as temperature increases.
The refractory-element addition maintains ductility at high temperature.
Compared with the baseline alloy, the modified alloy will have lower yield stress under high-temperature conditions.
Compared with the baseline alloy, the modified alloy will have improved creep resistance under high-temperature conditions.
Lower yield stress combined with improved creep resistance will result in controllable plastic deformation.
A nickel-based superalloy without tungsten or molybdenum additions exhibits less predictable elevated-temperature plastic deformation.
The proposed effects are significant only at high temperatures where dislocation climb and creep dominate.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the addition inhibits dislocation motion and impedes creep while also predicting lower yield stress. It does not explain how impeded dislocation motion produces the asserted yield-stress reduction, leaving the mechanism-to-outcome relation internally unresolved.
